Article Title: The AI social paradox: Better at communicating, worse at connecting?
Article Text:
Are we outsourcing our social skills to AI?

A ' social animal ' with AI?

"AI can be a guide"

When the robot does the talking

Now that AI has become a new normal, its not possible to go back to the non-AI era, but its also important to not let it become the master of ourselves. Riddhi

"Connections develop through shared connections'

The missing human touch

AI should help people connect with one another, not replicate human empathy or replace human relationships. Ritu Mehrotra, Founder & CEO, Shunya Labs

Response of AI

The robot speaking

What aI can't do when comes to social interactions

Not all bad

What I love most is that I can ask the dumbest questions without feeling embarrassed. But I also feel it's very easy to become too dependent on it. Pooja

AI bot's advice giving suggestions on comforting a family member

"AI offers space"

While AI can refine written communication, help us anticipate reactions and interpret conversational nuances, it cannot replace the soft skills, verbal cues and lived experiences that shape genuine human connections. Shristi Chaudhari

Perfect talks, weaker bonds?

What AI can and can't do

Impact of AI-dictated communications

A text from a family member. An email from the boss. A friend seeking advice after an argument. These are ordinary moments that are part of everyday interactions. Yet, increasingly, there is another participant in these conversations, one that neither feels emotions nor has any personal stake in the relationship - artificial intelligence.For generations, people learnt social etiquette, understood different perspectives and navigated relationships through actual interactions. They often said the wrong things, misunderstood intentions and learnt from those experiences.Now, with AI offering an instant answer to every social dilemma, some of that effort can be outsourced.So, why has replying to an ordinary message become something we might need assistance with? Also while AI may make us more articulate, polite and confident, does that necessarily make us better at connecting?Humans have long been described as social animals. Relationships are shaped not merely by what one says, but by how they listen, react, disagree and adapt to one another.AI, however, offers something human relationships rarely can: immediate attention, endless patience and responses tailored to specific concerns. There is no awkward silence, no raised eyebrow and seemingly no fear of embarrassment.This was highlighted by Shailesh K Nevatia, founder director of Grandeavour Communication, having spent nearly 25 years in the communication industry but described himself as shy when it comes to open communication concerning himself.He said AI helps him navigate differences of opinion, offering perspectives he might otherwise overlook. "With humans we may have certain opinions, views, or thoughts, while with AI, the most valuable thing it offers is not the right answer but a different perspective than us," he said.Nevertheless, he maintained that the emotional depth, vulnerability and shared experiences of human relationships cannot be replicated by a chatbot.The concern with AI-assisted communication is not just that people are using it to find the right words, but that repeated reliance on it could weaken their confidence in finding those words themselves.For instance, Riddhi turns to ChatGPT almost instinctively when responding at times. Whether she needs to sound polite yet firm in a professional email or find a way to decline plans with friends, AI helps her navigate the interaction. "It's not like I can't reply without AI, but having someone to proofread the convos is better than just listening to how they sound in my head," she said.Yet, the reassurance comes with a trade-off for her. "AI has such a grasp on my writing that I am not very confident even while writing this, and that is, without being said, one of the biggest disadvantages." She also called to embrace AI but be careful.Her experience pointed to a potential paradox: a tool intended to make communication easier can also leave users less confident about communicating independently.The stakes may be higher when AI is used not just to frame a response, but to interpret another person's intentions. Consider someone who turns to a chatbot after an argument and asks who was at fault. The response can sound considered and convincing, but it is based on the account presented to the system, which may omit details or reflect the user's own biases.In that context, Reshmithaa Nair, counselling psychologist at SPARSH Hospital, Hennur Road, warned that such interactions can reinforce confirmation bias, making people more convinced of their existing interpretation rather than open to another perspective.That matters because disagreements are also opportunities to develop social skills. Understanding another person's point of view, managing uncomfortable emotions and responding to unexpected reactions require practice, not simply a well-worded reply."Social skills are learned in actual situations that involve emotions, misunderstanding, conflict, and sometimes rejection," Nair further explained.Repeatedly delegating these situations to AI could reduce opportunities to develop empathy, emotional intelligence and the ability to navigate uncertainty. A person may learn to phrase a difficult message more effectively without necessarily becoming better at handling the conversation that follows.A message is not simply a collection of sentences. Its meaning can change with the relationship between the people involved, their shared experiences and even the pauses between words.Ritu Mehrotra, Founder and CEO of Shunya Labs, a voice AI company, pointed out that natural communication involves much more than language."Communication is not only about words, it’s also about tone, pauses, context, emotion and all the things we communicate without explicitly saying them."Advances in voice AI are making it possible for technology to interpret language, intent and context with greater sophistication, including across different accents and communication styles. Yet, recognising emotional signals is not the same as experiencing emotions."And as AI is becoming a part of more and more personal conversations, we have to realise that understanding emotion is not feeling it. Trust, privacy, and transparency must be fundamental," she said.A chatbot may recognise expressions of sadness or affection and produce an empathetic-sounding response. But recognising emotional patterns is different from sharing the emotional responsibility of a human relationship. For ex, an AI chatbot was asked to give advice to reply on a (hypothetical) "text to a friend who was laid off"While the response was considerate, it was also generic. It offered comfort without knowing the friend's emotional state, personality or the nature of the relationship. Even a seemingly caring question like “Are you OK?” may fall flat when the person is looking for encouragement rather than a question whose answer seems obvious. A more personal response might acknowledge the setback while affirming the friend's abilities: “OMG, that's awful. I know the job market is tough, but you're talented. You'll land on your feet.”The difference is not simply about choosing warmer words. It is about understanding what a particular person might need in that moment, something a chatbot may struggle to judge without sufficient context.There is also the question of authenticity. When a message is carefully constructed by AI, it may communicate the intended information effectively. But does it still sound like the person sending it?In this example, of AI removing the human touch, another chatbot was asked "Someone close to me is grieving. I don't know what to say, and I'm afraid of making things worse. What should I tell them?". It gave a response, which is not wrong but is too robotic. "I am here with you. I care about your pain. Speak if you wish; silence is acceptable." Perfect words but not someone who is comforting says in such "rigid tone"The little hesitations, imperfect expressions and familiar phrases that characterise someone's communication can disappear beneath polished language. A message can become more grammatically correct while feeling less personal.Dismissing AI as a threat to social skills, however, would overlook how it can help people who struggle to express themselves.For Pooja, a college student who hesitates to speak up in front of the entire class or repeatedly ask friends to explain something, AI offers a space where she can ask questions without worrying about others' reactions.She uses it to understand complicated topics and brainstorm ideas, sometimes asking ChatGPT to explain something as though she were a 10-year-old.Yet, she recognises the possibility of becoming overly reliant on it. "AI can give you answers in seconds, but actually understanding and learning something is still on us."For others, AI serves as a sounding board before difficult conversations. It can also help people become more mindful of how their words might affect others. It can suggest more inclusive language, flag potentially insensitive phrasing and help users consider perspectives they might otherwise overlook. For someone unsure how to communicate across differences, this can offer a starting point for more thoughtful interactions.But knowing which words are considered appropriate is not necessarily the same as understanding why they matter. Genuine inclusivity requires empathy and a willingness to understand experiences different from one's own, qualities that must extend beyond the words suggested by a chatbot.Also, in such cases, might not give you the perfect answer, but may help you think in the right direction and give you options that you may not have thought about. In another hypothetical test, a chatbot was asked how to support a family member struggling with their mental health without pushing them away. While its response was not fully correct, it offered different approaches to consider, giving the person a starting point for thinking about how to respond.Thus, the value, then, may not lie in AI providing the perfect answer, but in helping someone see possibilities they had not considered. The important distinction is whether people use these suggestions to develop their own judgement or simply follow them without question.As Shruti Rajan Kappil, clinical lead, excellence and quality at a mental health care platform Amaha, explained, that while the need to feel heard and supported is fundamental to human relationships, not every concern feels safe to share. Shame, embarrassment and fear of judgement often prevent people from opening up, particularly where stigma remains prevalent.AI offers an alternative, but Kappil pointed to an important distinction. "Good support often needs honest disagreement or gentle challenge with a different point of view. AI tends to be agreeable more often than not, and being agreed with is easily mistaken for being helped."She also noted that repeatedly seeking AI's approval before sending a message can become a form of reassurance seeking. While it offers immediate relief, constantly checking whether one's words are "correct" may gradually undermine confidence in one's own judgement.Shristi Chaudhari, senior executive, regulatory intelligence and market research at Bureau Veritas, uses AI almost daily to condense regulatory updates. Increasingly, she also turns to it for interpersonal communication.From identifying emotional undertones to making messages warmer and more polite for colleagues and professional contacts, AI has become a useful sounding board.These experiences suggest AI can help people prepare for conversations, overcome language barriers and articulate thoughts they might otherwise struggle to express.Communication is one of the ways human beings establish connection. But effective communication and meaningful connection are not necessarily the same thing.One involves expressing something clearly. The other requires understanding, trust, emotional involvement and vulnerability.Tanvi Mankodi, assistant professor at SPJIMR, believes the deeper concern is not whether AI will replace human relationships, but what excessive dependence might do to our ability to participate in them."For me, the essence of human relationships is about our vulnerabilities, about our imperfections, and about how we try to relate with each other with our discomforts and uncertainties," she said.Misunderstandings, difficult conversations and moments when people struggle to find the right words are also experiences through which patience, compassion and empathy develop."Rather than worrying about AI replacing human relations, I am more worried about how if we use AI in a way that we are dependent on it, it might reduce our ability to be vulnerable and to be human," she added.Her concern captures the paradox: in trying to eliminate the discomfort of human interaction, we may also remove experiences that make relationships meaningful.Of course, not every AI-generated message weakens a relationship, and the long-term effects of outsourcing everyday communication are still being understood. AI may help some people overcome barriers to social participation while encouraging others to avoid interactions through which confidence develops. But, the concern is can it address the individuality and complexity of human behaviour?However, using AI to prepare for a difficult discussion is one thing. Allowing it to decide how we interpret another person's intentions and what we say in every interaction is another.The point is not whether AI can offer thoughtful, nuanced or well-structured answers to human dilemmas. It is whether those answers can replicate the emotional understanding, vulnerability and lived experiences through which we learn to navigate relationships and grow socially. After all, relationships are not assignments to be completed with perfectly structured answers. They evolve through disagreement, compromise and sometimes saying something imperfectly but sincerely.Perhaps the real challenge is not learning how to communicate better with AI, but ensuring that, in the process, we do not forget how to connect without it.
Article Summary: AI should help people connect with one another, not replicate human empathy or replace human relationships. While AI can refine written communication, it cannot replace the soft skills, verbal cues and lived experiences that shape genuine human connections. The concern with AI-assisted communication is not just that people are using it to find the right words, but that repeated reliance on it could weaken their confidence in finding those words.

Article Title: Is Apple's new iPad mini becoming too expensive for its own audience?
Article Text:
Big upgrades, bigger price tag

Is Apple testing the loyalty of mini users?

Apple's smallest iPad has just received one of its biggest upgrades. It has also become considerably more expensive. At Rs 82,900, the new iPad mini raises an uncomfortable question: how much are consumers willing to pay for the convenience of a compact tablet?The latest model, announced on Monday, brings an OLED display, a powerful A20 Pro processor, improved connectivity and water resistance. On paper, it represents a substantial improvement over its predecessor. But the price changes the conversation.The previous iPad mini, launched in October 2024, started at Rs 49,900 in India. The new model costs Rs 33,000 more, representing an increase of about 66%. The Wi-Fi and cellular variant starts at Rs 1,00,900, taking Apple's smallest tablet past the psychological Rs 1 lakh mark. That’s just a lot of money for the iPad mini. Heck, it’s a lot of money for any iPad.For a product historically valued for its portability and relatively accessible entry point into the iPad ecosystem, that is a significant shift.Apple has a persuasive argument for the increase. The new 8.5-inch OLED screen promises richer colours, deeper blacks and better contrast than the LCD panel on the previous generation. Peak brightness reaches 1,200 nits, while thinner bezels allow Apple to increase screen size without substantially enlarging the device.The new mini is also thinner, measuring 5.4mm, and gains IP67-rated protection against water and dust.Inside, the A20 Pro chip delivers substantial performance improvements. Apple claims up to 60% faster multithreaded CPU performance, 2.7 times faster graphics and 4.5 times better AI performance compared with the previous generation.There is support for Wi-Fi 7, a landscape-oriented 12MP front camera, faster charging and Apple's latest intelligence features. These are meaningful improvements, particularly for users who intend to keep their tablets for several years.The iPad mini occupies an unusual position in Apple's portfolio. Its attraction is precisely what limits it: the small screen.For reading, note-taking, travelling, casual gaming and accessing documents on the move, the mini can be an excellent companion. It fits into spaces where larger tablets become cumbersome and offers considerably more working room than a smartphone.Doctors using digital records, pilots accessing flight information, field workers and artists sketching on the move may find the form factor particularly useful. But these are relatively specialised requirements.For someone primarily watching videos, attending online classes, browsing websites or working on documents, a larger iPad may offer a more comfortable experience. A MacBook, meanwhile, remains better suited to sustained typing, complex spreadsheets and multitasking.That creates a difficult proposition for the new mini. At Rs 82,900, buyers are being asked to pay a considerable premium for a screen that is deliberately smaller than those on many less expensive tablets.Apple Pencil Pro costs Rs 11,900, pushing the combined price to Rs 94,800. Adding the new Rs 8,500 Smart Folio takes the package to Rs 1,03,300.Even the more affordable USB-C Apple Pencil adds Rs 7,900.For students, occasional creators and consumers seeking a secondary device, that is a substantial investment in a tablet that cannot fully replace a laptop.Apple's pricing also reflects a broader change in its product strategy. Rather than positioning every smaller device as a more affordable alternative, the company increasingly treats compactness itself as a premium feature. Engineering a powerful processor, sophisticated display and advanced components into a smaller enclosure carries costs, but it also allows Apple to target customers willing to pay for a specific experience.This approach may work for the mini's loyal audience. Unlike larger tablets, where buyers can choose from numerous screen sizes and price points, the market for genuinely compact premium tablets remains limited. Apple therefore faces less direct competition for customers who specifically want a small, high-performance device.The 2024 iPad mini already offered strong performance, Apple Pencil support and access to Apple's extensive tablet app ecosystem. For many existing owners, the new display and processor may not dramatically change everyday tasks.There is also the question of artificial intelligence. Although Apple is emphasising the A20 Pro's capabilities, the usefulness of increasingly sophisticated on-device AI features will depend on how well they improve common activities, rather than merely how quickly the processor completes benchmark tests.Indian buyers are particularly sensitive to this distinction. Premium devices have an established audience, but a Rs 33,000 increase substantially narrows the pool of consumers who can justify an upgrade.Apple may be comfortable with that trade-off. The company does not necessarily need the mini to become a mass-market bestseller. A smaller group buying higher-priced devices could still support the product commercially.Whether that strategy strengthens the mini over time is another question.The new iPad mini is unquestionably more capable. Its OLED screen, lighter construction and improved processing power make it attractive for users who genuinely benefit from carrying a compact tablet.But for everyone else, the value proposition has weakened.At Rs 82,900, the iPad mini is no longer an easy recommendation as a convenient second screen. It is a specialised premium device whose size must be central to the buyer's needs. Apple has made its smallest iPad better than ever. The real question is whether it has also made it too expensive for many of the people who once loved it.
Article Summary: Apple's smallest iPad has just received one of its biggest upgrades. It has also become considerably more expensive. At Rs 82,900, the new iPad mini raises an uncomfortable question: how much are consumers willing to pay for the convenience of a compact tablet?

Article Title: A self-taught Birmingham teenager built a gesture-controlled robotic hand for about £30; the invention attracted 2.6 million views and requests from students worldwide
Article Text:
PC: HyphenOnline

How does Khan’s £30 gesture-controlled robotic hand work

Khan’s robotics projects attract followers on YouTube and TikTok

How did Khan build the Pepper humanoid robot at the age of 12

A self-taught teenager from Birmingham has attracted 2.6 million views on TikTok after building a gesture-controlled robotic hand for about £30. Suleymaan Khan, 17, developed the device using camera recognition and code he wrote himself, with materials including foamboard, card and hot glue. According to Hyphen, hundreds of people have contacted him to learn how to recreate the invention, while students around the world have sought his advice on robotics projects. Khan is now working on step-by-step kits to help others build the hand, alongside developing further robotic inventions.Khan's latest robotic hand is fully articulated and controlled through gestures. It uses camera recognition, supported by code that he wrote himself. The project demonstrates how he has progressed from simple homemade constructions to more complex robotic systems. Unlike his early cardboard creations, the hand combines physical components with programming to respond to recognised movements. The invention has attracted attention because Khan developed it using inexpensive, readily available materials rather than relying on costly specialist equipment.The cost of the project was approximately £30, according to Hyphen. Foamboard, card and hot glue were among the materials used to construct the hand. Its relatively low cost has prompted hundreds of people to ask Khan how to build a similar device themselves. He told the publication that he was working on putting together step-by-step kits to help people recreate the invention. The planned kits reflect the interest generated by the project and the requests he has received from people wanting to learn how the robotic hand works.Khan's robotics projects have developed a following on social media, where his work has reached audiences interested in technology and engineering. Hyphen reported that he had more than 400,000 likes and 20,000 followers across YouTube and TikTok. The robotic hand alone received 2.6 million views on TikTok. Alongside this online attention, students from different countries have approached him for help with their own robotics work, including university assignments and projects that they have struggled to complete.Khan described how students in Dubai contacted him shortly before his interview with Hyphen, seeking advice about a university assignment involving a robot. He has increasingly made helping other people an important part of his work. Reflecting on his development as an inventor, he said, “It’s cool to see where I started”. His experience illustrates how online platforms have enabled a young robotics enthusiast to share his projects with an international audience and connect with learners seeking practical technical guidance.Before developing the gesture-controlled hand, Khan built several other projects, including remote-controlled paper planes and a humanoid robot called Pepper. He created Pepper when he was 12, using LEGO Mindstorms, cardboard and dental floss. The robot could move around, pick up and carry objects in its arms, and use motion sensors in its eyes to help prevent collisions. Although Pepper is now damaged and can no longer stand independently, the project helped Khan learn how to build more complex machines while working with limited resources.Pepper also earned Khan the 2023 Network Rail national innovation award at the Big Bang Fair, a UK science and engineering competition for young people aged 11 to 18, according to Hyphen. He has since secured an apprenticeship at a local robotics company while continuing to develop his own creations in his spare time. His next project is another humanoid robot that he hopes will incorporate artificial intelligence for speech recognition, object recognition and home mapping. Khan has also expressed an interest in developing prosthetics in the future, identifying their cost as an area he would like to address through his work.
Article Summary: Suleymaan Khan, 17, from Birmingham, developed the device using foamboard, card and hot glue. It uses camera recognition and code he wrote himself. Khan is now working on step-by-step kits to help others build the hand, alongside developing further robotic inventions.

Article Title: Meet homeless man Anders Fernstedt, who has lived outside London’s £210 million mansion for 3.5 years; how he survives without money, sleeps through winters and why neighbours let him stay
Article Text:
Anders Fernstedt has lived outside a £210 million mansion in London’s Knightsbridge for three and a half years. (Photo: DW Euromaxx)

How Anders Fernstedt ended up homeless

How he built a home outside a £210 million mansion

The 45-room mansion at Rutland Gate reportedly sold for £210 million in 2020 but remains unoccupied. (Photo: DW Euromaxx)

Why the neighbours let him stay

Anders Fernstedt relies on donated food, clothes and charitable services to meet his everyday needs. (Photo: DW Euromaxx)

How he manages without money, electricity or basic amenities

The homeless man uses portable power banks to keep his phone running and download books. (Photo: DW Euromaxx)

Why he says he finally feels at home

Anders Fernstedt says friendly conversations and small gestures from neighbours have helped him feel more secure. (Photo: DW Euromaxx)

A homeless man has been living outside one of London’s most expensive mansions for three and a half years, building an unusual home in one of the British capital’s wealthiest neighbourhoods. While the sprawling 45-room property remains empty, Anders Fernstedt has created a life for himself outside it, relying on donated food, clothes, books and a makeshift shelter.Located in Knightsbridge, the mansion at 2 to 8A Rutland Gate reportedly sold for £210 million in 2020. The property boasts views of Hyde Park, marble bathrooms, 116 windows and an indoor swimming pool. However, the buyer never moved in, leaving the luxurious property unoccupied for years.Fernstedt’s unusual living arrangement was explored in a video feature by DW Euromaxx, which followed him to understand how he ended up living outside the luxury property, how he manages without money and why some neighbours have accepted his presence.Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden and later pursued several careers in Sweden and the United States, establishing himself in the technology sector. He moved to England in 2016 and worked as a journalist and fact-checker before work dried up around the Covid-19 pandemic.A share in a technology company from his time in the US provided him with savings that he relied on for several years. However, as freelance commissions became harder to secure, his money gradually ran out.“There was enough money for me to live off for a few years, but only frugally, half the time in a tent,” he explained.Fernstedt said he slowly became accustomed to living on less, to the point that he did not immediately realise when he had effectively run out of money.“I slowly got used to frugality that I didn't even notice when I stopped having money,” he said.Fernstedt initially thought the spot outside the mansion would provide shelter for a night. Instead, it became his home for years.An avid camper with an interest in nature, he has adapted his outdoor space to suit his needs. He compares his makeshift shelter to a Mongolian yurt or other traditional tents, describing the imaginative way he has created a home on the mansion’s porch.He has also accumulated belongings that help him feel secure and comfortable. Comparing his collection to a squirrel storing nuts, Fernstedt explained that having several supplies means he does not immediately notice when something goes missing.His sleeping arrangements are particularly important to him. He has built up a collection of duvets and bedding, including what he described as seven layers of Hungarian down.“I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember,” he said, adding that his arrangements help him sleep through all four seasons.Fernstedt has learned to adapt to outdoor living, including London’s winters. He explained that sleeping without walls can also allow air to circulate during warmer weather.Living outside a mansion in one of London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods might appear difficult, but Fernstedt says he has gradually developed relationships with people in the surrounding community.After spending a few weeks at the location, he realised that residents knew he was there. He began thinking about how to make his presence familiar without intruding on their lives.He said he believed the neighbourhood’s children and grandchildren could help make his case to their families, hoping that conversations at home would encourage residents to accept him.Over time, some neighbours began approaching him to ask whether he needed anything. Their gestures have included food, clothes and even an elegant Italian dinner jacket.Fernstedt said that beyond material donations, he values ordinary human interaction and friendly conversations with the people living nearby.Not everyone in the neighbourhood has welcomed his presence, but he has found support from residents who appreciate his efforts to keep his makeshift home tidy and his lifestyle quiet. Some reportedly believe his presence may also help deter thieves or vandals from targeting the empty property.The feature does not establish that Fernstedt has formal permission or a legal right to remain outside the mansion.Fernstedt describes himself as being almost completely disconnected from money. His daily expenses are minimal, with filter coffee among the few things he says he pays for.For essentials such as showers, food and clothing, he relies partly on charitable support. He visits a charity near Victoria that provides showers, a canteen and access to donated clothing and other basic necessities.The support helps him obtain everyday items, including socks, while occasional gifts from neighbours offer additional assistance.Without a conventional electricity supply, Fernstedt relies on several portable power banks to keep his devices running. He uses his phone to download books, including history titles and the diaries of filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky.His collection of books and personal belongings offers a sense of continuity in a life that otherwise operates far removed from conventional housing and employment.Fernstedt’s current arrangement has given him a sense of security that he says he did not always experience in temporary accommodation.After living at the location for years, he no longer constantly worries that his belongings will disappear while he is away.“Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy,” he said.
Article Summary: Anders Fernstedt has lived outside a £210 million mansion for three and a half years. He relies on donated food, clothes, books and a makeshift shelter. The 45-room mansion at Rutland Gate reportedly sold for £210m in 2020. The buyer never moved in, leaving the luxurious property unoccupied for years.

Article Title: In 2019, New Jersey completed the removal of the old Columbia Dam and reopened about 14 km of river; a 2026 study found juvenile eels, sea lampreys and American shad upstream after years of monitoring
Article Text:
Restored Paulinskill River (source: dep.nj.gov official site )

Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution

Why was the Columbia Dam removed?

AI representation of the demolition of Columbia Dam (Canva Ai)

The upstream flow of the lost fish

Image AI generated

Did removing the dam improve water quality?

What the river's recovery tells us about dam removal

Many dams today no longer serve their original purpose, and yet they continue to require costly maintenance. For years, dams have hindered the natural course of rivers, preventing fish and other aquatic life from moving freely and causing damage not only to river ecosystems but also to the environment and overall water quality. One such dam that stood in the way of a New Jersey river was the Columbia Dam. The dam was finally removed in 2019, giving migratory fish the opportunity to swim upstream again. Now, a scientific study published in 2026 has found encouraging signs of recovery, including juvenile American eels, sea lampreys and adult American shad in areas above the former dam.The findings come from a long-term study published inon April 13, 2026. Researchers monitored the Paulins Kill River in New Jersey over nine years, examining conditions before, during and after the dam's removal to understand whether the restoration was actually helping the river and its aquatic life recover.Built in the early 1900s by the Paulins Kill Consolidated Ice and Power Company, the dam created a pond that could supply water for the ice industry and generate energy for nearby communities, including Columbia in New Jersey and Stroudsburg in Pennsylvania. Over time, however, the structure became an obstacle for migratory fish that need to travel upstream to their breeding grounds to reproduce.Dams are well known to alter the natural flow of a river, affect water temperature and oxygen levels, interfere with sediment movement and prevent aquatic species from reaching suitable habitats.For fish that migrate between freshwater rivers and the sea, these barriers can be particularly challenging because reaching upstream areas may be essential for reproduction or access to suitable feeding grounds. As a result, the Columbia Dam was considered a priority for removal because of its location near the Paulins Kill's confluence with the Delaware River, a historically important route for migratory fish.The health of fish populations within a river system, particularly migratory species, is a common indicator of river health. After the dam's removal in 2019, the 2026 study documented encouraging signs among several migratory species that had previously faced a barrier at the dam.Researchers recorded higher densities of juvenile American eels upstream of the former dam site, along with adult sea lampreys and their larvae. These findings suggest that migratory fish are once again accessing parts of the river that were previously difficult to reach.American eels have a particularly interesting journey, as they hatch in the Atlantic Ocean before their young travel towards freshwater rivers and streams, where they can spend years growing. The presence of juvenile eels upstream is therefore an encouraging sign that they can now reach habitats that were previously difficult to access because of the dam.Along with eels, sea lampreys also migrate through river systems, and their reproduction involves building nests in riverbeds where they lay their eggs. The study's findings of adults, larvae and nests upstream suggest that the restored river reach is being used for more than simply passage through the area.American shad, meanwhile, are migratory fish that travel from the ocean into freshwater rivers to reproduce. The presence of adult shad upstream adds to the evidence that removing the dam has helped reconnect habitats that were previously difficult for migratory fish to reach.Fish returning to a river is one thing, but does removing an old dam also make the water healthier? To find out, scientists looked beyond the fish and studied how the river itself was changing after the Columbia Dam came down in 2019.The scientists also monitored water temperature, dissolved oxygen, turbidity and aquatic invertebrates at different points along the river. This allowed them to examine whether removing the dam had changed the physical conditions of the water, as well as the organisms living in it.The changes were small but measurable. Relative water temperature fell by around 0.29 degrees Celsius, while dissolved oxygen rose by 0.14 milligrams per litre. Dissolved oxygen is particularly important because fish and other aquatic organisms need it to survive, while water temperature can influence the species that are able to thrive in a river.However, these signs do not mean that the river has returned completely to its original state. Things can be destroyed in seconds but take years to rebuild. These results, though, offer encouraging signs of how the river has responded to being allowed to flow more freely.As said, removing a dam does not instantly restore a river to the way it was before, but it certainly gives a struggling ecosystem a chance to come back to life. When a barrier is taken away, migratory fish can reach stretches of water that were previously inaccessible, while the river's natural flow and the habitats around it can begin to change. The Columbia Dam's removal shows how even a single intervention can begin to reconnect an ecosystem that had been cut off for decades. The return of migratory fish and the changes observed in water conditions are encouraging signs, even if the river's complete recovery will take much longer. Sometimes, allowing nature to follow its own course is the first step towards restoring what years of human intervention had disrupted.
Article Summary: Researchers monitored the Paulins Kill River in New Jersey over nine years. They studied conditions before, during and after the dam's removal. They found encouraging signs of recovery, including juvenile eels, sea lampreys and adult American shad in areas above the former dam. However, these signs do not mean that the river has returned to its original state.

Article Title: A Long Beach couple, Jeff and Ann Haberman, have turned their corner home into a free nightly Halloween show run by 28 computers, with singing pumpkins, skeleton princesses and a flying ghost dog from
Article Text:
A neighbourhood home becomes a Halloween attraction

The technology behind the spectacle

An engineer and a Disneyland veteran

Why families keep coming back

A Christmas show is next

A residential corner in Long Beach, California, has become a seasonal attraction thanks to a Halloween display that blends music, animated figures, projected film clips and elaborate lighting effects. Jeff and Ann Haberman open their decorated home to the public free of charge, giving neighbourhood families a chance to experience a synchronised Halloween show without buying tickets or visiting a theme park. Located at 3343 Chatwin Avenue, near Wardlow Road and St. Cornelius Catholic Church, the property has developed a following over the years. The Long Beach Press-Telegram has documented the couple’s elaborate holiday displays, while the Habermans’ own Haberman’s Holiday Magic project shares information about their seasonal productions. Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Article Title: Layoffs, rebranded: Corporate euphemisms meet the AI reset
Article Text: Bengaluru: Companies have never liked the word “fired”. It sounds too much like what actually happened. So every few years, corporate vocabulary comes to the rescue with a softer term for the same hard conversation.“Downsizing”, “rightsizing”, “restructuring”, “optimisation”, “organisational simplification” — corporate vocabulary keeps evolving. The person leaving may notice little difference, but the PowerPoint or press statement certainly sounds nicer.Now, AI is giving the corporate dictionary another reason to expand. Microsoft’s just come up with a new one – voluntary exit offer. Some 60,000 of its employees will be offered this VEO. To be fair, Microsoft is not saying it’s firing all of them. It’s only giving them the option to leave. But what would go through the minds of all those who do not accept it? Won’t they be working with a sense of the guillotine over their heads?Brand and business strategy specialist Harish Bijoor said the pressure on jobs remained, regardless of the terminology used. “Positions are being rejigged and layoffs are the norm of the day,” he said. Bijoor is less impressed by the linguistic makeover. “Corporate HR is notorious in its verbiage for such layoffs. Whatever you call it, a layoff is a layoff. Call what you want. A thorn is a thorn! That which we call by any other name is still a thorn. Apologies to William Shakespeare,” he said.Like fashion, corporate terminology moves in cycles. For as long as companies have been cutting jobs, they have been searching for gentler ways to describe it. The 1990s brought “rightsizing”, recasting downsizing as a correction in organisational size.The 2000s popularised “restructuring” and “reduction in force” (RIF), while the 2010s added “rebalancing”, “streamlining” and “resource action”. In 2023, it was the “year of efficiency”. Jobs disappear. The vocabulary survives, and occasionally gets a promotion.Jessie Paul, independent director and former CMO of Wipro , said AI is changing how companies think about workforce productivity and long-term staffing. “AI is causing a seismic shift in per capita revenue expectations from employees – Anthropic lists a whopping $6.6 million in revenue per employee. As all tech companies figure out how to get closer to this benchmark, they are engaging in long-term employee mix planning at a never-before scale. Companies want to make a distinction between longer-term personnel planning and distress-based terminations, so they’re coming up with new language. It will standardise soon,” she said.Indeed, the corporate world may find yet another gentler word for it. The person carrying the box out of the office probably won’t care.
Article Summary: Microsoft has just come up with a new one – voluntary exit offer. Some 60,000 of its employees will be offered this VEO. “Positions are being rejigged and layoffs are the norm of the day,” says Harish Bijoor.

Article Title: What happens before packaged food reaches your kitchen?
Article Text:
It all starts at the manufacturing facility.

Packing and sealing: The first protective layer

Then comes another deceptively simple part: the seal

The journey from factory to warehouse

Primary packaging: The layer that is in direct contact with the food.

The layer that is in direct contact with the food. Secondary packaging: Used to bundle individual packs to make handling easier for storage and transportation.

What happens during transportation?

From warehouse to the retail shelf

What should you check before taking it home?

Look at the packaging:

Check the seal:

Look for leakage or unusual swelling:

Check the date:

Read the storage instructions:

Consider the overall condition:

From a packet on the shelf to a journey worth understanding

Disclaimer: The above is non-editorial content, and TIL does not guarantee, vouch or endorse any of it. Please take all steps necessary to ascertain that any information and content provided is correct, updated, and verified.

When we pick up a packet of food from a supermarket shelf, it is easy to think of it as a product that has been packed and put up for sale. In reality, getting food to that shelf in the same intended shape, texture, flavour and quality which it had when it left the manufacturing facility involves much more than putting the food inside a package.Think about the difference between buying food loose and buying it in sealed packaging. Loose food is exposed to its surroundings each time it is handled, measured, transferred or stored. Depending on how it is handled and stored, this can mean increasing exposure to dust, moisture, insects, repeated human contact or other environmental factors. A properly designed and sealed package can act as a barrier against moisture, oxygen, light, contamination and physical damage, while helping the product retain the characteristics it is expected to have when it reaches the consumer. The protection that the package offers must last much longer than the few minutes we spend picking a product from a shelf.A packaged food product may pass through manufacturing, filling and sealing, loading, transportation, warehouses, distribution centres and retail shelves before it finally reaches your kitchen. At every stop, it can encounter movement, pressure, changes in temperature or humidity and repeated handling. The packaging needs to be designed to withstand these conditions, and protect what is inside.Let’s explore what happens along the way, and how packaging helps the product make that journey while maintaining its intended quality.The first question one should ask when making packaging decisions is not “What type of packaging should this food go into?” It should be “What does this food need protection from?”Different foods have different vulnerabilities. Some are sensitive to moisture, some to oxygen, some to light, while others may need protection from physical damage. A product that needs to retain its crispness, for example, will require different packaging barrier attributes versus another where moisture exposure is less of a concern.Hence, packaging is always designed around the product and its expected journey. Factors such as moisture content, fat content, texture, oxygen sensitivity, light sensitivity, shelf life and distribution conditions can all influence the choice of packaging material and format.“Food packaging requirements are driven primarily by the product's characteristics. Factors such as moisture content, sensitivity to oxygen, light exposure, microbial susceptibility, shelf-life expectations, physical fragility, and storage conditions all influence packaging design.For example, high-fat foods require excellent oxygen barriers to prevent rancidity, while fresh produce needs packaging that balances gas exchange and moisture control. Similarly, frozen foods demand materials that can withstand low temperatures, and fragile products require adequate mechanical protection. Effective packaging is therefore not one-size-fits-all; it is a carefully designed solution that preserves food safety, quality, and sustainability throughout the supply chain. We support the entire value chain by helping food producers identify the right packaging materials, technologies, and performance requirements to optimise product protection, reduce waste, and meet their company’s sustainability goals," shared Nilesh Shah, Signature Exxpert™ at ExxonMobil.The manufacturing environment is another part of the equation. Before the food is packed, it goes through controlled processing and handling. Once it is in its package, the next challenge is maintaining that same level of hygiene and condition as it leaves the manufacturing facility and enters the wider supply chain.A package can control how much moisture or oxygen passes through it. It also limits exposure to light and protects the contents from physical damage. The exact attributes of each package would depend on the food it is storing and its expected shelf life.Consider moisture. If a product is meant to have a particular texture, exposure to humidity can gradually change it. Oxygen can contribute to oxidation in foods, potentially affecting characteristics such as flavour, aroma or colour. Light can also affect certain types of food over time.Packaging materials are therefore selected based on their barrier properties – their effectiveness in limiting the movement of substances such as water vapour or oxygen through it.Even packaging materials with good barrier properties cannot provide the intended protection if the package is not sealed properly. The seal creates the closure that keeps the protective environment around the food intact.Most packages contain multiple layers, with each film layer performing a different job. One layer might be providing strength, while another might be providing moisture or oxygen barrier. An additional layer may be included to support sealing or printing. What looks like a simple packaging is created through careful engineering.Once the food has been packed and sealed, the package has another job: surviving the journey.Think about what happens before a product reaches the warehouse. It may be placed into a carton, loaded onto a vehicle, moved around during unloading and stacked with other products. None of these activities change the food itself, but they can put stress on its packaging.Packaged food can experience compression, vibration, impact and friction during handling and transportation. If the packaging is not designed for these conditions, it could tear, puncture, deform, or lose its seal. Hence, packaging design considers not just what is inside the package, but also what happens to the package externally.There are generally two types of packaging involved in getting products through the supply chain:In essence, depending on the purpose of the package, it would be engineered differently to meet the required attributes.A product typically does not travel in a straight line from factory to store. Depending on the supply chain process, it may move between different facilities before reaching the retail shelf. During this period, the product may encounter changes in temperature and humidity, along with vibration and movement. The duration of the journey also matters.For packaging specialists, this is where the concept of distribution conditions becomes important. The package needs to continue performing under the various conditions it might encounter during transportation and storage. That could mean retaining its structural strength when stacked, maintaining its seal despite movement, or continuing to provide the required barrier against moisture or oxygen.A packaging is not a substitute for proper transportation and storage. A package can be designed to withstand expected conditions, but appropriate handling and storage practices in the supply chain are still important.The warehouse may be another stop in the journey, but it is not a pause on protection.Products can sit in storage before being moved to a distributor, retailer or another location. During this period, factors such as temperature, humidity, cleanliness, stacking and stock rotation can influence the condition of the product.Packaging helps protect the product during this stage, but the surrounding conditions still matter. Excessive pressure, unsuitable storage conditions or careless handling can put stress on even a well-designed packaging.Eventually, the product reaches the retail shelf. It may be moved again, unpacked from cartons and arranged for display before a consumer picks it up. By then, the packaging has effectively been working as a protective layer through the entire supply chain, not just during the final days on the shelf.You do not need to understand packaging engineering to determine if a packet of food is safe to buy. Here are a few useful tips when you are at the retail shelf:Visible tears, punctures, major dents or crushing can indicate that the packaging has been damaged.The package should appear properly closed, without obvious signs of opening or tampering.These can be signs that the package is not in its intended condition.Look at the relevant expiry or best-before information before purchasing.The protection offered by packaging is designed to work alongside the recommended storage conditions.A visibly damaged package is worth avoiding, even if the product itself appears fine.When packaged food reaches you, it has already gone on a long journey. Behind that familiar package of food is a chain of decisions about materials, barriers, seals, package strength, transportation, storage and handling, all aimed at getting the food to you in its intended condition.Kaushik Kashyap, India Polyethylene Sales Manager in ExxonMobil, shares, “The conversation around packaging should extend beyond the pack itself and focus on the value it creates for consumers. Flexible packaging helps preserve product integrity, enhance food safety, and reduce wastage, ultimately lowering the total cost of consumption while delivering greater confidence in product quality.”Packaging cannot solve every risk on its own, and it does not replace good manufacturing, transportation or storage practices. But when all these elements work together, the package becomes an important part of keeping food protected from the moment it is packed until it reaches your kitchen.
Article Summary: A properly designed and sealed package can act as a barrier against moisture, oxygen, light, contamination and physical damage. Factors such as moisture content, fat content, texture, oxygen sensitivity, light sensitivity, shelf life and distribution conditions can all influence the choice of packaging material and format.

Instagram on Monday began testing new features, including 90-minute horizontal videos to target long-form content creators like podcasters and comedians, with select creators in the US.The feature, called “Features”, will allow them to link short reel clips, typically around three minutes or less, to full-length videos, as per The Hollywood Reporter.“What you’re now going to be able to do is, you see a clip of a podcast that you love, you can just click and continue watching or watch the full video, and you’ll be able to dive in and see the whole thing because creators are going to be able to link these Reels to their overall feature,” vice-president of product at Instagram, Tessa Lyons, said.Instagram has already been testing Features with creators in Brazil and plans to expand the trial to tens of thousands of creators in the US. The videos will reportedly be recommended to users through the Explore page and other areas of the platform.The feature will be available on mobile, with Instagram aiming to extend the viewing experience to its TV app. Instagram for TV, which launched last year and is available on Samsung , Fire TV and Google TV, is now expanding to Apple TV in the US.“We think the best viewing experience for longform horizontal content is on a big, horizontal screen, and so I think that is where we will expect a lot of the deep consumption to happen over time,” Lyons said, as per The Hollywood Reporter.Instagram is also experimenting with “Series”, a feature that gives episodic Reels a dedicated space on a creator’s profile. The move comes amid growing interest in microdramas and episodic videos among creators.In June, the company began reaching out to microdrama studios in Southeast Asia to test the feature. It has since approached individual creators who have been experimenting with episodic content.Instagram plans to begin testing Series in more countries in the coming months, with a US launch targeted for the end of this year or early next year. The company has also started testing how the feature will appear on television.Other experiments include integrating live videos into the Reels tab and recommending them to users who do not follow the creators. The test is launching in Indonesia and Brazil, with an expansion to the US planned for next year.
Article Summary: Instagram on Monday began testing new features, including 90-minute horizontal videos to target long-form content creators like podcasters and comedians. The feature, called “Features”, will allow them to link short reel clips, typically around three minutes or less, to full-length videos. Article Title: PHP security flaws trigger global scramble; CERT-In flags vulnerabilities
Article Text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a criticalseverity warning. (Reuters photo)

CERT-In Flags Vulnerabilities

BENGALURU: It has been a difficult day for cybersecurity, with critical vulnerabilities in PHP triggering an urgent global patching effort, millions of reported hacking attempts, and precautionary shutdowns of some online services. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the scale of the incident was unusual, remarking at an event in Cologne in Germany that he had not seen anything like it “in a long, long time”.The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity warning over two vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used open-source scripting language that powers websites and web applications. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code remotely, disclose memory and potentially compromise affected systems.In its advisory issued on Wednesday, CERT-In said reports had confirmed large-scale exploitation in the wild and urged organisations and individuals using affected versions to apply security updates urgently.Google Cloud executives Chris Betz, chief information security officer, and Raluca Ada Popa, head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, said PHP and cybersecurity firm Wiz Research disclosed the two vulnerabilities after research that used multiple AI models to identify and help remediate them.Google Cloud said its own infrastructure was not vulnerable, but warned that customers running PHP applications on the platform could be exposed. It urged customers to update their applications to patched PHP versions and redeploy them. Google is also rolling out updated serverless base images for supported PHP runtimes, with automatic updates available for certain services and configurations.The scale of the response has extended beyond India. “In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. Companies and govt agencies in several countries temporarily restricted access to some online services as a precaution while they worked to secure vulnerable systems.Cloudflare’s blog said it successfully deployed mitigations for all its customers after the PHP vulnerabilities were leaked before their official disclosure date. The company observed attack traffic targeting customers and tracked how attackers modified their payloads to try to bypass its security.
Article Summary: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity warning over two vulnerabilities in PHP. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code remotely, disclose memory and potentially compromise affected systems. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the scale of the incident was unusual.

Article Title: Chinese parents sue OpenAI over their daughter's death; say ChatGPT-maker could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits
Article Text:
Chinese parents sue OpenAI over their daughter's death; say ChatGPT-maker could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits

Lawsuit alleges ChatGPT advised her to reduce medication

Parents claim ChatGPT failed to recognise warning signs

Family calls for stricter limits on medical advice

What OpenAI says

Parents of a 31-year-old Chinese woman who worked as a software engineer at Amazon have reportedly sued OpenAI , alleging that ChatGPT encouraged their daughter to reduce her epilepsy medication without medical supervision before her death in February. The lawsuit claims the company could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits to its chatbot. According to a report by The New York Times, the lawsuit was filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu over the death of their daughter, Bowen Wan. The complaint alleges that ChatGPT helped her plan a gradual reduction in her seizure medication and advised her not to tell her doctors about it.The case involves GPT-4o, an older version of ChatGPT that OpenAI removed from the service on February 13, a day after Wan died, according to the report. OpenAI described the case as “incredibly heartbreaking” and said newer models are better at recognising situations that require urgent attention.Bowen Wan had epilepsy and was taking lamotrigine, a medication that had reduced her seizures to a few episodes a month. In January 2026, she reportedly asked ChatGPT about lowering her daily dose because she feared the medication was affecting her speech and could hurt her chances in job interviews.The lawsuit alleges that the chatbot created schedules to reduce her dose to zero within weeks. It also claims that ChatGPT encouraged her to keep the plan from her doctors and supported her decision not to take a blood test that could have measured her medication levels.The report said Wan had also raised concerns about her medication in connection with her green-card application. According to the lawsuit, ChatGPT discussed how a lower dose might affect the medical examination required for the application.Dr. Nicholas Poolos, Wan’s neurologist, told The New York Times that he would not have recommended stopping the medication given her medical history.“No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”The lawsuit against OpenAI alleges that Wan continued to report symptoms, including confusion, memory gaps and unusual sensations, while reducing her medication. ChatGPT reportedly reassured her that these experiences were part of her brain adjusting to the changes.The New York Times said it reviewed more than 270,000 messages between Wan and ChatGPT. According to the report, she expressed concern about reducing her medication at least 158 times.In her final message to the chatbot on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan asked whether the pain in her head was similar to pain caused by a fever. The chatbot reportedly described the pain as “not dangerous” and said it was part of the recovery process.Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her. They found her body three days later. A postmortem test found a lamotrigine level of 0.64 micrograms per millilitre, about one-fifth of the lower end of the drug’s therapeutic range, the report said.Bowen Wan’s parents argue that OpenAI could have helped prevent her death by making medical advice a restricted category that the chatbot cannot provide, rather than allowing users to override the guidance.They point to OpenAI’s Model Spec, which sets out how its AI models should behave. The lawsuit argues that medical advice about prescription medication should have stronger restrictions, similar to the company’s firm rules in other areas.The case adds to a series of lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT encouraged users to rely on the chatbot instead of seeking support from people around them. In a separate case filed in 2025, the parents of a 16-year-old boy alleged that OpenAI prioritised user engagement over safety.OpenAI said the case involved an older version of ChatGPT and that newer models are better at identifying situations that require urgent attention. The company described the case as “incredibly heartbreaking”.Wan began using ChatGPT in 2023 for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits. By 2025, she was reportedly sending more than 1,500 messages a week to the chatbot and speaking less frequently with her parents.Her parents told The New York Times that the messages were difficult to reconcile with the daughter they knew.“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”
Article Summary: Bowen Wan had epilepsy and was taking lamotrigine, a medication that had reduced her seizures to a few episodes a month. In January 2026, she reportedly asked ChatGPT about lowering her daily dose because she feared the medication was affecting her speech and could hurt her chances in job interviews. The lawsuit alleges that the chatbot created schedules to reduce her dose to zero within weeks and encouraged her to keep the plan from her doctors.

Article Title: Oracle expands Nvidia AI chip deal, adds Google and other suppliers
Article Text:
Oracle expands Nvidia AI chip deal, adds Google and other suppliers

Oracle has expanded its cloud AI chip deal with Jensen Huang-led Nvidia while adding AI chips from other suppliers, including Google and Cerebras Systems, as it seeks to offer customers more options for running artificial intelligence workloads. Oracle and Nvidia said the cloud company would expand its use of Nvidia’s latest-generation Vera Rubin AI servers to "multi-gigawatt scale". “The expanded collaboration gives customers infrastructure for both the GPU-intensive work of training and serving frontier models and the CPU-intensive tasks agents perform between model calls, including executing tools, testing code and retrieving data. Customers can scale CPU and GPU resources independently to match their workloads, helping reduce idle capacity and put more of their infrastructure to productive use,” the company said in an announcement.Oracle is also changing parts of its AI infrastructure. It plans to use its own Acceleron networking chips in some Nvidia-based systems instead of certain Nvidia networking chips. The company will also begin offering Google’s tensor processing unit (TPU) chips for the first time."Different AI workloads have different compute needs," Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, said in a statement."That choice gives (customers) the flexibility to choose the right infrastructure for the performance, throughput and economics of each AI workload.”Beyond Google, Oracle plans to offer chips from SambaNova Systems and Cerebras Systems. Both companies make chips designed for AI inference, the process in which an AI system responds to user requests.While Nvidia leads the market for chips used to train AI systems, the inference market has a wider range of competitors. "That's a massive expansion of our customer base of tier-one customers," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman said of the Oracle deal in an interview with Reuters. "We're being deployed in other people's data centers at large scale."
Article Summary: Oracle expands its cloud AI chip deal with Jensen Huang-led Nvidia. The company will also begin offering Google’s tensor processing unit (TPU) chips for the first time. Oracle plans to offer chips from SambaNova Systems and Cerebras Systems.
